Indeed
ĭn-dēd'
adv. (in deed, in fact, in reality; the Authorized Version's word for the genuine article as against the nominal one)
Originally two words, in deed — that is, in act, as opposed to in word or in appearance. English fused them, and in fusing them nearly lost the contrast that gives the word its point.

Biblical Definition

Indeed distinguishes the real thing from the thing merely called by the name, and the New Testament uses it at some of its sharpest turns. Of freedom: “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36) — spoken to men who had just insisted they were never in bondage to any man, and who were at that moment slaves of sin. Of discipleship: “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31) — continuance, not initial profession, is what makes a disciple the real article. Of the Baptist: the chief priests dared not deny that “all men counted John, that he was a prophet indeed” (Mar 11:32) — and their fear of saying so out loud exposes them. In every case the word does the same work: it drives a wedge between the label and the substance, and it asks the reader which side of the wedge he is on. Nathanael receives the Lord's own use of it: “an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile”.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines indeed as in reality, in truth, in fact — and notes its use to denote concession, admission, or emphasis according to the sense.

expand to see more

INDEED, adv. [in and deed, in fact.] In reality; in truth; in fact.

The carnal mind is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. Rom. viii.

2. It is used to denote concession or admission; as, ye are indeed learned, but not wise.

3. It is used to note interrogation with surprise; as, is it indeed so?

Key Scripture

Joh 8:36 — "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."

Joh 8:31 — "Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;"

Mar 11:32 — "But if we shall say, Of men; they feared the people: for all men counted John, that he was a prophet indeed."

Deu 17:4 — "And it be told thee, and thou hast heard of it, and enquired diligently, and, behold, it be true, and the thing certain, that such abomination is wrought in Israel:"

Modern Corruption

Joh 8:36 is quoted for a freedom the passage explicitly denies — autonomy — when the freedom Christ names is freedom from the servitude of sin.

expand to see more

“Free indeed” is among the most misappropriated phrases in Scripture, printed over sentiments about self-determination and being true to oneself. The context is unambiguous: “Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin” (Joh 8:34), and the freedom offered is release from that bondage into the household of the Son. Nothing in the passage promises freedom from law, from authority, or from constraint. The men Christ is addressing believed themselves free already, which is exactly the condition the word indeed is inserted to puncture.

Joh 8:31 supplies the test the modern church most needs and least applies. Those addressed are described as having believed on Him, and the Lord immediately attaches a condition to the reality of their discipleship: if ye continue in my word. Continuance is the evidence, not the cause — but where there is no continuance, the New Testament does not encourage the profession to be treated as a disciple indeed. That is the doctrine of perseverance stated as a pastoral test, and it stands against the decisionism that counts a raised hand as a settled matter.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English in deed, in act; rendering Greek ontos (G3689), really, from the participle of eimi, to be, and alethos (G230), truly.

expand to see more

English in deed — in act, as opposed to in name or in word; the two words fused in Middle English.

Greek ontos (G3689) — really, actually; from on, the participle of eimi, to be. “Free indeed” is ontos eleutheroi — free in the order of being.

Greek alethos (G230) — truly, of a truth; “disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31) and “an Israelite indeed” (Joh 1:47).

Greek men — the concessive particle, often rendered “indeed” where a contrast with de follows: “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mat 26:41).

1Ti 5:3, 5 — “a widow indeed”, ontos chera, distinguishing the genuinely destitute widow from the one with family to keep her.

Usage

"“Free indeed” — freedom from the servitude of sin, not freedom from authority."

"“Disciples indeed” — continuance in His word is what makes the profession real."

"“A prophet indeed” — what the priests knew and would not say aloud."
